Excavate

/EKS-kuh-vayt/ - the stress falls on EKS · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Excavate means to dig out of the ground and remove.

Badgers had excavated a den under the shed, throwing out a fan of sandy soil overnight.

Worked Example

To seat the new telescope, engineers excavated a circular pit forty feet across in the mountain's granite crown, hauling the spoil down by cable car.

Excavate is more exact than dig because it includes the removal: the material is not just loosened but taken out and carried away, usually methodically and on a serious scale.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

unearth: dig up and bring to light — stresses the discovery

exhume: dig up from a grave, specifically

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bury: cover something over with earth

entomb: seal something away as if in a tomb

Where it sits · how big and systematic the operation — scoop → dig → excavate

scoop vs. excavate: Scoop is the smallest gesture — a trowel of loose soil lifted in a second.

dig vs. excavate: Dig is stronger than scoop but plainer than excavate: anyone can dig a hole, while excavating means digging material out and removing it, methodically and at scale.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: out

Root — cav

Root — cav: hollow (Latin cavus)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb ending: to make or do

Put it together

Put it together: Ex- (out) + cav (hollow, from Latin cavus) + -ate (verb ending) = to hollow out — to make a hollow by taking the material away. The root is easy to spot elsewhere: a cave is a natural hollow, a cavity is a hollow eaten into a tooth, and concave describes a surface that curves inward like a bowl.

Use the root in a new word: cavity

Use the root in a new word: cavity: The hygienist found one small cavity where a molar's grooves had trapped years of sweets.

Word Choice

neutral / technical

Excavate is the working word of crews and archaeologists: it promises method, scale, and removal — spoil actually leaves the hole. Plain dig covers a child with a stick; unearth spotlights the find rather than the labor. If the thing coming up is a body from a grave, English reserves exhume.
